title: Great Inventions · Episode 2
chapters: The safety lift: how Otis made skyscrapers possible

units.t: Great Inventions. Episode two.
In this episode: The safety lift: how Otis made skyscrapers possible, Telephone and radio, How photography was invented and How the movies began.
Part one. The safety lift: how Otis made skyscrapers possible.
Lifting people up a shaft was easy.
Convincing them they would not plunge to their deaths was the hard part, and one man did it by cutting his own rope.
Why lifts were deadly.
Lifting with ropes and pulleys is ancient.
Builders hauled stone, mines raised ore, and in Rome's Colosseum, wooden lifts worked by teams of men raised wild animals into the arena.
By the early nineteenth century, steam-powered hoists moved goods between factory floors.
People rarely rode them.
Hemp ropes wore out and snapped, and when they did, the platform and everything on it fell straight down the shaft.
A broken rope on a goods hoist meant smashed crates.
On a passenger lift it would mean funerals.
Building a lift that people would trust was the real challenge.
Otis's safety brake.
Elisha Otis was an American mechanic from Vermont who had tried businesses from wagon building to running a sawmill.
In 1852 he was working at a bedstead factory in Yonkers, New York, and was asked to help install a hoist to lift heavy equipment.
Worried about what would happen if the rope failed, he devised a safety brake.
He attached a strong wagon spring to the top of the platform, linked to the hoisting rope.
While the rope was taut, the spring was held in.
If the rope broke and the tension vanished, the spring snapped outwards and its ends caught in ratchet teeth cut into the guide rails on either side of the shaft.
All safe, gentlemen.
A clever brake is useless if nobody trusts it, and Otis understood showmanship.
At an exhibition in New York's Crystal Palace in 1854, he rode an open platform high above the crowd, then had an assistant cut the only rope with an axe.
The platform dropped a few centimetres and stopped dead.
Otis is said to have announced, "All safe, gentlemen, all safe."
Whether or not those were his exact words, the stunt worked, and orders arrived.
In March 1857 the first commercial passenger safety lift opened in the E.
V.
Haughwout Building, a five storey store on Broadway.
Steam-powered, it climbed about twelve metres a minute.
Otis died in 1861, but his sons built the company into a giant, with lifts around the world, including the Eiffel Tower.
Upside-down buildings.
Before lifts, buildings were limited by how many stairs people would climb, usually five or six storeys.
The top floors were the least desirable, often rented cheaply to servants, poor tenants or struggling artists.
Safe lifts changed that.
Combined with steel frames, which carry far more weight than thick masonry walls, they let cities build upwards, and the skyscraper was born.
Chicago's ten storey Home Insurance Building, finished in 1885, is often called the first.
Electric lifts soon replaced steam and hydraulic ones; Werner von Siemens demonstrated one in Germany in 1880.
The view, the quiet and the distance from street noise made the top floors the most prestigious addresses in town.
How lifts stay safe.
Modern traction lifts hang from several steel cables, each strong enough alone to hold the car.
A counterweight balances the car, so the motor lifts only the difference.
If the car goes too fast, an overspeed governor triggers brakes that clamp onto the guide rails, a descendant of Otis's idea.
Buffers cushion the car at the bottom.
In 1945, after a bomber hit the Empire State Building, operator Betty Lou Oliver survived a fall of about 75 storeys, partly because trailing cables and compressed air slowed it.
Supertall towers use sky lobbies, where passengers change lifts, and lighter carbon fibre cables.
If you ever get stuck, press the alarm or intercom button, stay inside and wait for trained help.
Never try to climb out.
For a medical emergency, call 000.
The key idea: People hoisted loads for thousands of years but avoided riding them, because a snapped rope meant a straight fall.
Part two. Telephone and radio.
In 1850 news from London took months to reach Australia.
Within one lifetime, voices crossed the world in a fraction of a second.
The wire shrinks the world.
The telegraph was the first electrical communication system.
Cooke and Wheatstone patented a practical version in Britain in 1837, and Samuel Morse, with Alfred Vail, developed a simpler system and the dot-and-dash Morse code.
In 1844 Morse sent 'What hath God wrought' from Washington to Baltimore.
A lasting Atlantic cable followed in 1866, after an 1858 cable failed within weeks.
News from Britain once came to Australia by ship and could take two months or more.
In 1872 the Overland Telegraph Line, built under Charles Todd, ran about 3,200 kilometres from Adelaide to Darwin and linked to an undersea cable from Java, connecting Australia to London.
Messages arrived within hours.
The line crossed the Country of many Aboriginal nations, with lasting effects on the people there.
Alice Springs grew around one of its stations.
Bell and the telephone.
Alexander Graham Bell, a Scottish-born teacher of deaf students, received a US telephone patent in March 1876.
Days later he reportedly called to his assistant, 'Mr Watson, come here, I want to see you.'
Credit remains disputed.
Elisha Gray filed on a similar design at the patent office the same day.
Antonio Meucci built voice-transmitting devices years earlier but couldn't afford to keep up his patent notice, and in 2002 the US House of Representatives honoured his work.
Many contributed; Bell won the legal battles.
A telephone is only useful if it connects, so networks grew around exchanges.
Human operators, very often women, connected calls by hand on switchboards.
Automatic exchanges appeared in the 1890s.
Melbourne opened an exchange in 1880, and by the late 20th century nearly every Australian home had a landline.
Marconi and radio.
Radio rests on science from the 1860s, when James Clerk Maxwell predicted invisible electromagnetic waves, and the late 1880s, when Heinrich Hertz proved they existed.
From 1895, Guglielmo Marconi turned this into practical wireless telegraphy, sending Morse code over ever greater distances.
In 1901 he claimed a signal across the Atlantic, though some historians doubt it was truly heard.
Others made key contributions, including Oliver Lodge, Jagadish Chandra Bose, Alexander Popov, Karl Ferdinand Braun and Nikola Tesla.
Marconi shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Braun.
A 1943 US Supreme Court ruling struck down some of Marconi's patent claims, but named no single inventor of radio.
Radio reaches Australia.
On 22 September 1918, Australia received its first direct wireless messages from Britain.

A message from Prime Minister Billy Hughes, who was then in Britain, was sent from Marconi's station in Wales and picked up roughly 17,000 kilometres away by Ernest Fisk at his home in Wahroonga, Sydney.
Fisk went on to lead the company AWA.
Regular broadcasting began in 1923, and radio soon became the nation's shared living room, bringing news, sport and serials.
In the outback, Alfred Traeger's pedal-powered radio, from 1929, let remote stations call the Flying Doctor, and later made the School of the Air possible.
Mobiles and shared credit.
On 3 April 1973, Motorola engineer Martin Cooper made the first call from a handheld mobile phone on a New York street.
His prototype weighed around a kilogram and offered only about half an hour of talk time.
Australia's first cellular network, an analogue service run by Telecom Australia, launched in 1987.
Digital networks followed in the 1990s, bringing text messaging, and smartphones from 2007 put the internet in our pockets.
Morse, Bell and Marconi are famous because they made ideas practical, won patents and built companies, not because they worked alone.
When a single name is attached to an invention, ask who else was working on the same problem.
Each leap changed society: the telegraph cut news times from months to hours, radio created mass audiences, and mobiles made people reachable almost anywhere.
The key idea: The telegraph sent coded messages almost instantly, and the Overland Telegraph Line connected Australia to Britain in 1872.
Part three. How photography was invented.
For thousands of years, people could watch an image of the world appear in a darkened room but had no way to keep it.
Then chemistry caught up.
Picture in a dark room.
Darken a room completely and make a small hole in one wall, and an upside-down image of the outside world appears on the opposite wall.
This effect, the camera obscura, Latin for dark room, was described by thinkers in ancient China and Greece and studied carefully by the Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham around 1,000 years ago.
By the Renaissance, portable versions with lenses and mirrors helped artists trace scenes accurately.
But the image vanished the moment the light changed.
Capturing it permanently needed a material that changed when light hit it, and a way to stop that change once the picture was made.
Solving those two problems took until the nineteenth century.
The first photographs.
In about 1826 or 1827, French inventor Nicéphore Niépce put a bitumen-coated pewter plate in a camera at a window of his country house.
Bitumen hardens in light.
After an exposure of many hours, possibly days, he washed away the unhardened parts, leaving a faint image of buildings and rooftops.
View from the Window at Le Gras is the oldest surviving camera photograph.
Because the sun moved during the exposure, buildings on both sides look lit.
After Niépce died in 1833, his partner, the Parisian showman Louis Daguerre, developed a faster process.
A silver-coated copper plate was sensitised with iodine fumes, exposed, then developed with toxic mercury vapour.
The result was stunningly detailed, but each image was unique and could not be copied.
In 1839 the French government acquired the rights and announced it to the world.
Negatives and copies.
In England, William Henry Fox Talbot was working on his own method at the same time.
He used paper soaked in silver salts, which darkened in light, to make negatives, images with light and dark reversed.
By shining light through a negative onto another sheet of sensitive paper, he could make a positive print, again and again.
His improved process, the calotype, was patented in 1841.
Calotypes were softer and less detailed than daguerreotypes, but the negative and positive principle was the future.
Almost all film photography for the next 150 years followed Talbot's idea.
One of his earliest surviving negatives, from 1835, shows a window at his home, Lacock Abbey.
Photography spreads.
In 1851, Frederick Scott Archer introduced the wet collodion process: glass plates that gave fine detail and copies, with exposures of seconds.
Photographers carried portable darkrooms to coat and develop each plate while wet.
Photography recorded war, from the Crimean War to the American Civil War, and portrait studios let many families afford a likeness.
An 1845 daguerreotype of Sydney doctor and politician William Bland is among Australia's earliest surviving photographs.
Photography was still fiddly until George Eastman launched the Kodak camera in 1888, sold loaded with film for about 100 pictures.
Customers posted the camera back for developing and reloading.
The slogan: "You press the button, we do the rest."
The 1900 Brownie box camera cost one dollar in the United States and put photography within reach of ordinary families.
Colour, then digital.
Early colour was difficult.
The Lumière brothers released the Autochrome process in 1907, using dyed grains of potato starch to make dreamy colour images on glass.
Easier colour film, such as Kodachrome, launched in 1935.
Then came a bigger shift.
In 1975 Kodak engineer Steven Sasson built an experimental digital camera.
It was about the size of a toaster, captured black and white images of just 0.
01 megapixels and recorded them onto cassette tape.
Kodak did not push the technology hard, partly because film was so profitable, and the company filed for bankruptcy protection in 2012.
Today billions of people carry a camera in their phone, and well over a trillion photos are taken every year.
The key idea: The camera obscura projected images for centuries before anyone could capture one.
Part four. How the movies began.
A question about a galloping horse, a peephole machine and a café screening in Paris led to the most popular art form of the twentieth century.
And one of the first feature films was Australian.
The galloping horse.
For centuries, painters showed galloping horses with legs stretched out front and back like a rocking horse.
Nobody could see fast enough to know.
In California, the businessman Leland Stanford hired the photographer Eadweard Muybridge to find out whether all four hooves ever left the ground at once.
In 1878, Muybridge set up a row of cameras along a track, triggered one after another as the horse raced past.
The pictures showed that the hooves did leave the ground, but when they were tucked under the body, not stretched out.
Muybridge then put his sequences on a spinning disc and projected them, so audiences watched the horse appear to run.
Moving pictures had begun.
The illusion of motion.
A film strip is a long row of photographs, each slightly different from the last.
Shown quickly enough, the brain stops seeing separate pictures and perceives smooth movement.
This was long explained by persistence of vision, the idea that each image lingers on the retina.
Most researchers now think that is incomplete.
The illusion mainly comes from how the visual system detects motion, filling in movement between closely spaced images, an effect psychologists call apparent motion.
Early silent films ran at varied speeds, often around 16 to 20 frames per second.
When sound arrived in the late 1920s, 24 frames per second became the standard, and it is still common today.
Peephole versus screen.
Thomas Edison's laboratory, with much of the work done by his assistant William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, used flexible celluloid film with holes punched along the edges.
Their Kinetoscope, shown to the public in 1894, was a wooden cabinet with a viewing hole.
One customer at a time peered in at a film lasting less than a minute: a strongman flexing, dancers, a sneeze.
Edison thought individual viewing would be more profitable, which let rivals take the lead in projection.
In France, Auguste and Louis Lumière built the Cinématographe, a light, hand-cranked machine that could film, print and project.
On 28 December 1895, beneath the Grand Café in Paris, they showed short scenes from life to a paying audience.
The tale of viewers fleeing their train film has little reliable evidence.
Stories on screen.
Georges Méliès, a Paris stage magician, discovered that stopping the camera, changing something and restarting could make people vanish.
His 1902 film A Trip to the Moon became one of early cinema's most famous images.
In 1903, Edwin S.
Porter's The Great Train Robbery told an action story across separate scenes, and audiences learned to accept cuts.
In 1906, a Melbourne team including the Tait family filmed the bushranger Ned Kelly's story.
The Story of the Kelly Gang ran about an hour, far longer than almost anything before, and is widely considered the first feature-length narrative film.
Most of it is lost, since early nitrate film was fragile and flammable.
Fragments restored by the National Film and Sound Archive joined UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007.
The talkies arrive.
Silent films were rarely silent.
Cinemas hired pianists, organists or whole orchestras, and some used narrators or sound effects.
But recording dialogue that matched the actors' lips was hard.
In 1927 Warner Bros released The Jazz Singer, with synchronised songs and a few spoken lines.
Audiences were thrilled, and within a few years most studios had switched to sound.
The change was brutal for some.
Actors whose voices did not suit the microphone lost careers, cinema musicians lost jobs, and cameras were temporarily trapped in soundproof booths.
Yet sound also opened new forms, such as the musical.
In barely three decades, moving pictures had gone from scientific curiosity to global art.
The key idea: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed a running horse in sequence, showing that all four hooves leave the ground, tucked under the body.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did people avoid riding hoists before Otis?
Answer. A snapped rope sent the platform plunging down the shaft.
Question two. How did the Overland Telegraph Line change Australia's links with Britain?
Answer. Messages took hours, not weeks by ship.
Question three. What problem did early camera obscura users face?
Answer. The image vanished when the light changed.
Question four. What did Muybridge's photographs reveal about galloping horses?
Answer. All four hooves leave the ground, legs tucked under.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
